extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal education funds, school administrators, LEAs, and legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal rationale explaining the scope of Title IX's prohibition on sex discrimination and the Department's reasons for including specified bases (and excluding others) in §106.10 of the final regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of specified bases in §106.10
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.10 clarifies that Title IX's prohibition on sex discrimination includes discrimination on the bases of sex stereotypes, sex characteristics, pregnancy or related conditions, sexual orientation, and gender identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department states it is important to clarify that Title IX's prohibition includes these bases and supports that position with Supreme Court and circuit case law (e.g., Bostock; Price Waterhouse; Grabowski; Grimm; Whitaker; Nevada Dep't of Hum. Res. v. Hibbs). The text explains these bases are examples of discrimination that involve consideration of a person's sex.

rubrics_metrics.name: No separate regulatory definition of 'sex' required
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department determined that providing a specific definition of 'sex' for purposes of §106.10 is unnecessary for these regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As explained, discrimination on the listed bases is sex discrimination because each necessarily involves consideration of a person's sex even if 'sex' is understood narrowly (e.g., biologically) as assumed in Bostock. The Department relies on prior explanations in the July 2022 NPRM and related case law to justify not defining 'sex' in §106.10.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listed bases are illustrative, not exhaustive
rubrics_metrics.description: The bases listed in §106.10 are examples intended to provide notice of Title IX's broad scope and are not an exhaustive list of all forms of sex discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department rejects the contention that noting the list is not exhaustive deprives recipients of notice. It explains that many laws and policies use example lists to clarify scope, and nothing in the final regulations prevents recipients from adopting policies that include additional examples or training to further clarify applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 'bases' of discrimination and 'forms' of discriminatory conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.10 describes bases of discrimination (what the discrimination is based on); forms of conduct (e.g., sex-based harassment, sexual violence) are distinct and are addressed elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department disagrees with suggestions to add specific forms of conduct into §106.10, emphasizing that 'sex-based harassment' and 'sexual violence' are examples of discriminatory conduct, not bases. This distinction is reflected in the definition of 'sex-based harassment' in §106.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage includes discrimination based on perceived status
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.10 extends to discrimination based on a perceived status, whether the perception is accurate or not (e.g., perceived sex, perceived sexual orientation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department cites Title VII/Title IX and case law (Abercrombie & Fitch; Roberts v. Glenn Indus.; Jones v. UPS; EEOC v. WC&M Enters.; Grabowski) to show that discrimination predicated on perceptions violates anti-discrimination law and that courts often use Title VII precedent to inform Title IX interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex characteristics includes intersex traits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department interprets the regulatory term 'sex characteristics' to include 'intersex traits' and declined to add 'intersex' separately to §106.10.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department refers to its NPRM explanation that 'intersex' describes people with variations in physical sex characteristics and states adding 'intersex traits' separately is unnecessary because they are encompassed by 'sex characteristics.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Marital status is not a per se prohibited basis under Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declined to add 'marital status' to §106.10 because discrimination based solely on marital status does not necessarily require consideration of a person's sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, the Department clarifies that Title IX prohibits treating individuals differently on the basis of sex in rules concerning marital status (e.g., treating married women differently than married men). The preamble cites specific regulatory cross-references (§106.21(c), 106.37(a)(3), 106.40(a), 106.57(a), 106.60) as examples where marital-status-based rules that effectuate sex discrimination are covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may adopt further clarifying policies and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the final regulations prevents a recipient from adopting policies that include examples of prohibited conduct or from providing training to clarify the scope of Title IX's coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department expressly invites recipients who want further clarity to supplement the regulations with local policies and training materials, noting the regulations provide adequate notice without specifying outcomes for every factual scenario.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key definitional language is placed in §106.2; preamble shorthand not regulatory
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department uses terms in the preamble (e.g., 'LGBTQI+,' 'transgender,' 'intersex') for convenience and explanation, but these terms are not part of the regulatory text; key terms are defined as necessary in §106.2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble provides conceptual descriptions (e.g., transgender: sex assigned at birth differs from gender identity; intersex: variations in physical sex characteristics) but stresses that rights and obligations under the final regulations depend on the regulatory text and §106.2 definitions, not preamble shorthand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department's statutory authority to promulgate §106.10
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department asserts authority under 20 U.S.C. 1682 (and related statutes) to issue regulations effectuating Title IX's nondiscrimination mandate, including regulations addressing sexual orientation and gender identity as forms of sex discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department supports its authority with statutory citations and case law (Gebser; Jackson; Bostock; Price Waterhouse; Oncale), explains the administrative enforcement mechanisms authorized by Title IX, and rejects commenters' claims that such regulation exceeds delegated authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of Title VII jurisprudence to Title IX interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts' interpretations of Title VII often inform interpretation of Title IX, and the Department relies on Title VII precedents (e.g., Price Waterhouse, Oncale, Bostock) to justify inclusion of sexual orientation and gender identity as forms of sex discrimination under Title IX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble cites multiple decisions and explains that Bostock's reasoning about sex-based discrimination applies in Title IX contexts and that more recent federal court decisions applying Bostock to Title IX are persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative law and procedural compliance (APA/notice-and-comment and non-retroactivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department states it complied with APA notice-and-comment requirements for this rulemaking and that the final regulations apply only to sex discrimination alleged to have occurred on or after August 1, 2024 (no retroactive enforcement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department responds to a district court preliminary injunction related to a prior Notice of Interpretation, explains that the injunction addressed notice-and-comment, not statutory authority, and notes recipients always have the option to decline federal funding rather than comply with post-acceptance conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: PPRA (Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment) compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department disagrees that §106.10 violates PPRA, noting the PPRA's requirements relate to certain surveys and that the final regulations do not require recipients to administer surveys or ask students to disclose 'sex behavior or attitudes' or religious practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble cites PPRA provisions (20 U.S.C. 1232h(b)(3), (7); 1232h(c)(1)(B), (2)(B), (2)(C)(ii)) and explains that §106.6(g) reinforces parental or guardian rights to act on behalf of children where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: EO 12866 / compelling public need justification for regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: In response to commenters, the Department explains that the persistence of discrimination on the listed bases presents a compelling public need and that commenters' evidence supports the regulatory decision under Executive Order 12866.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department rejects arguments that the NPRM lacked substantial evidence, citing enforcement experience and commenters' examples of discrimination and impacts on educational access as sufficient justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal preemption when State law conflicts with Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department explains that recipients' obligations to comply with Title IX and these final regulations are not obviated by conflicting State or local laws; federal statutes and regulations can preempt State laws when compliance with both is impossible or State law stands as an obstacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble cites Supreme Court precedents on preemption (Freightliner Corp.; Hillsborough Cnty.; Planned Parenthood of Hous.; O'Brien) and explains that nothing in these regulations prevents States from adopting policies consistent with Title IX but that conflicting State laws may be preempted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of constitutional rights (First Amendment) in application
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department clarifies that nothing in the Title IX regulations requires a recipient to restrict rights guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution (including the First Amendment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 106.6(d) makes explicit that the Title IX regulations do not authorize restrictions on constitutionally protected speech, and the Department reiterates that other provisions likewise do not authorize such actions.
